text: Claims that a viral video shows a natural disaster have often been traced back to unrelated footage from a different country or an earlier event.
Health claims that a single food or supplement cures a serious disease are almost always unsupported by peer-reviewed clinical evidence.
Statistics shared without a named source, dataset, or methodology are a common marker of fabricated or exaggerated claims.
Quotes attributed to public figures that do not appear in any official transcript, interview, or press release are frequently fabricated.
Claims describing a breaking event with no coverage from any established news outlet after several hours are often premature or false.
Headlines using urgent, emotionally charged language ('SHOCKING', 'THEY DON'T WANT YOU TO KNOW') are a common pattern in low-credibility content designed to drive clicks over accuracy.
